extracted.intended_audience: immigration attorneys, regulated parties (aliens/obligors), bond issuers, policy analysts, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Text of DHS's proposed public-charge rule (Sept 21, 2018) describing public-charge inadmissibility criteria, required forms, public charge bond procedures (posting, substitution, cancellation, breach), fees, and the rule's estimated economic impacts. Intended for stakeholders to review and comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge determination: prospective, totality of circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarifies that evaluating public charge is a prospective determination based on the totality of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS proposes to prescribe how it determines whether an alien is inadmissible because he or she is likely at any time to become a public charge; the determination is prospective and considers the totality of the circumstances (see proposed 8 CFR 212.22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum and additional factors for public charge determinations; positive and negative weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlines minimum and additional factors considered when evaluating whether an alien immigrant is inadmissible based on the public charge ground. Positive and negative factors are weighed to determine an individual's likelihood of becoming a public charge at any time in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule formalizes and standardizes criteria and process for public charge determinations, specifying which factors are considered and that they may be weighed positively or negatively depending on their impact on likelihood to become a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation methodology for monetizable non-cash benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides the methodology for calculating the annual aggregate amount of the portion attributable to the alien for the monetizable non-cash benefits considered in the public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule establishes how to value certain non-cash benefits for inclusion in public charge analysis (see proposed 8 CFR 212.24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions and waivers for public charge inadmissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlines exemptions and waivers for inadmissibility based on public charge grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adds a regulatory provision (proposed 8 CFR 212.23) describing categories of applicants who are exempt or eligible for waiver from the public charge ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to submit Form I-944 with Form I-485 (and potential RFEs for other forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS would require adjustment applicants subject to the public charge inadmissibility ground to submit Form I-944 with their Form I-485 to demonstrate they are not likely to become a public charge. Form I-129, I-129CW, and I-539 beneficiaries/filers may also be required to file Form I-944 if issued an RFE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule would impose new costs and time burdens because applicants must complete Form I-944; USCIS may exercise discretion to issue RFEs to require Form I-944 for nonimmigrant filings (sensitivity analysis estimated costs for 10–100% RFE rates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of self-sufficiency and evidentiary requirements for adjustment applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend 8 CFR 245 to require aliens submit a declaration of self-sufficiency on the form designated by DHS and any other evidence requested in the public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form I-944 functions as the declaration of self-sufficiency; DHS may request additional evidence as part of the public charge determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond: USCIS discretion to approve, set bond schedules, cancellation, substitution, duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Set forth the Secretary's discretion to approve bonds, cancellation, bond schedules, and breach of bond, and move principles governing public charge bonds to proposed 8 CFR 213.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed changes to 8 CFR 103.6 and 213.1 will establish when DHS may accept a public charge bond, minimum amounts required, substitution rules, cancellation procedures, and how bonds are administered for aliens seeking adjustment of status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of bond breach: collection of full bond as liquidated damages
rubrics_metrics.description: If USCIS determines that the bond has been breached, DHS proposes that USCIS would collect on the bond in full, meaning the total monetary amount of the bond as liquidated damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from legacy INS practice (forfeiture only of amount of public benefits received). DHS explains total damages are difficult to calculate precisely and liquidated damages are appropriate and historically used in immigration bond cases; a final breach determination creates a claim in favor of the United States that may not be released by an immigration officer (see proposed 8 CFR 213.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals and parties: who may appeal breach determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the obligor appeals a breach determination, procedures under 8 CFR part 103 apply; if appeal is dismissed/rejected or obligor fails to appeal, the breach determination becomes final and USCIS may issue a demand for payment. The alien may not appeal the breach determination or file a motion because the bond contract is between the obligor and the U.S. government; the alien is not a party to the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 8 CFR 103.3(a)(2), 103.5 and practice manuals; references that an immigration bond is a contract between the Service and the obligor (Matter of Ins. Co. of N. Am.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion of administrative remedies before federal suit
rubrics_metrics.description: A party must first exhaust all administrative remedies and obtain a final decision from USCIS in accordance with 8 CFR part 103 before being able to bring suit challenging USCIS cancellation or bond breach determination in Federal district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states courts review bond breach determinations under the Administrative Procedure Act; exhaustion requirement is proposed at 8 CFR 213.1(j).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond processing fees and fee structure
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to charge $25 for the posting of a public charge bond, $25 for posting a substitute public charge bond, and $25 when the alien, obligor or co-obligor requests to cancel the public charge bond (Form I-356).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INA section 286(m) authorizes DHS to set fees to recover costs; DHS proposes these nominal fees ($25) to recover at least some costs and notes no option to request a fee waiver for these fees; additional fee estimates include $34,234 annual total cost to obligors for I-945 and $825 annual total for I-356 filers (based on unit costs * estimated populations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surety bond fees and concurrent surety-bond rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees paid to surety bond companies to secure public charge bonds could range from 1–15 percent of the public charge bond amount based on an individual's credit score. DHS simultaneously published a separate proposed rule (June 5, 2018) establishing procedures and standards under which DHS would decline surety immigration bonds from Treasury-certified companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The June 5 proposed rule would also create administrative exhaustion requirements applicable to sureties; DHS plans to conduct the two rulemakings concurrently, and a final public charge rule may depart from the June 5 rule with respect to surety bond breach determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee-setting authority, IEFA funding, and limitations on cost recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: INA section 286(m) authorizes DHS to set fees for adjudication/naturalization services at levels ensuring recovery of full costs. Fees collected are deposited into the Immigration Examinations Fee Account (IEFA) and used to fund processing and related services. USCIS reviews IEFA fees biennially and may propose adjustments; the proposed $25 fees will not result in recovery of the full cost of intake and adjudication for Forms I-945 and I-356.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS cannot currently estimate start-up costs or expected bond volumes and will adjust fees after obtaining operational data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory planning and review requirements and economic significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 13771 direct agencies to assess costs and benefits, quantify effects, reduce costs, and maximize net benefits. This proposed rule is designated a 'significant regulatory action' and OMB reviewed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS provides summary estimates of annual and 10-year costs and benefits, follows OMB Circular A-4 accounting and prepared an A-4 accounting statement (Table 37).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantified economic impacts and transfer payment estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS estimates annualized quantified new direct costs ranging from about $45.3 million to $129.6 million, 10-year undiscounted costs of $453.1 million to $1.296 billion, and estimates reductions in federal/state transfer payments (approx. $2.27 billion annually) due to disenrollment or foregone enrollment in public benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS provides specific line-item cost estimates (e.g., increased time burden for Forms I-485, I-129, I-129CW, I-539; costs to obligors for I-945 and I-356 filings), discount-rate scenarios (3% and 7%), and calculations for transfer payment impacts and state shares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory familiarization costs and reading time assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS estimates individuals or entities would need approximately 8 to 10 hours to read and become familiar with the proposed rule; these familiarization costs are considered direct costs if incurred by regulated parties and indirect costs if incurred by other stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of entities likely to read the rule include immigration lawyers, advocacy groups, health care providers, non-profits, and religious organizations; DHS assumes opportunity cost of time as part of the economic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected qualitative impacts: increased denials and downstream effects
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS anticipates a likely increase in the number of denials for adjustment of status applicants based on public charge inadmissibility determinations due to formalizing and standardizing criteria and process; potential downstream impacts include lost productivity, adverse health effects, additional medical expenses, and impacts on businesses and service providers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS flags qualitative/unquantified effects on Medicaid providers, pharmacies, grocery retailers (SNAP), agricultural producers, landlords participating in federal housing programs, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFE practice and sensitivity analysis for RFE-triggered Form I-944 filings
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS adjudication officers may exercise discretion to issue RFEs whereby beneficiaries/applicants of Forms I-129, I-129CW, or I-539 may have to submit Form I-944; DHS conducted a sensitivity analysis estimating costs for a range of 10% to 100% of beneficiaries/filers receiving such RFEs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS provides estimated annual cost ranges for affected categories: Form I-129 beneficiaries $6.09M–$60.86M; Form I-129CW beneficiaries $0.114M–$1.141M; Form I-539 applicants $3.164M–$31.644M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical changes to CFR references and form names
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to new provisions, the proposed rule would make technical changes to 8 CFR 103.6 to update references to offices and form names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are editorial/technical updates to reflect the new public charge bond process and associated forms.
